Through the Objective 21 of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM), States committed to cooperate in facilitating safe and dignified return and readmission, as well as sustainable reintegration. Safe and dignified return and sustainable reintegration are an indispensable part of a comprehensive approach to migration management. Assisted voluntary return (AVR) programs aim to support migrants who are unable or unwilling to remain in host or transit countries and wish to return to their countries of origin. The main beneficiaries of IOM’s return and reintegration assistance are stranded migrants in host or transit countries, irregular migrants, asylum seekers who decide not to pursue their claims or who are found not to be in need of international protection, and migrants in vulnerable situations, such as victims of trafficking, unaccompanied and separated children, or migrants with health-related needs. IOM views reintegration to be sustainable when “returnees have reached levels of economic self-sufficiency, social stability within their communities, and psychosocial well-being that allow them to cope with (re)migration drivers. Having achieved sustainable reintegration, returnees are able to make further migration decisions a matter of choice, rather than necessity”. This definition highlights the multidimensional nature of a reintegration process – economic, social and psychosocial – and the need to approach migrant reintegration in a comprehensive manner, considering the factors that can affect reintegration at the individual, community and structural levels. Most migrants return to Amhara, Oromia, Tigray, and Central Ethiopia regions, often to remote communities where IOM has minimal presence. This position will be based in Jimma zone, Oromia region, close to beneficiaries, to bring IOM closer to beneficiaries and strengthen IOM’s capacity to deliver. The sub-unit works closely with government counterparts, service providers and partners to strengthen national capacities for reintegration, ensure protection-sensitive programming for vulnerable groups, and contribute to addressing the drivers of irregular migration and re-migration. Established in 1984 and operating in over 45 countries, we respond to emergencies, tackle poverty, empower communities, and advocate for lasting change. We are seeking an experienced and strategic Regional Finance Controller - Africa (West and East) to join our Finance & Corporate Services Division. This is a unique opportunity for a senior finance leader who is passionate about financial governance, capacity building, compliance, and driving sustainable improvement across complex international operations. title: RESPONSABLE DU BUREAU DE PLAIDOYER ET DE LIAISON AUPRÈS DE L’UNION AFRICAINE, Oxfam en Afrique
description:
Type de contrat : Contrat à durée déterminée de 2 ans Grade interne : B1, International Rémunération : conforme à la grille salariale d’Oxfam International. Cette offre comprend les avantages sociaux de base ainsi que les prestations globales applicables au personnel recruté à l’international et relocalisé.Nous considérons que les modalités de travail flexibles sont essentielles pour bâtir le Secrétariat de demain. Nous sommes donc disposés à échanger avec vous sur les modalités susceptibles de vous convenir. Le poste Oxfam en Afrique recherche une personne expérimentée, dotée d’un leadership reconnu et d’un forte capacité d’influence, pour diriger son Bureau de plaidoyer et de liaison auprès de l’Union africaine (UA), basé à Addis-Abeba. En tant que membre de l’Équipe de direction de la Plateforme Afrique, vous piloterez l’engagement d’Oxfam auprès de l’Union africaine et de ses institutions. Vous élaborerez et mettrez en œuvre des stratégies de plaidoyer à fort impact afin d’influencer les politiques et les pratiques à l’échelle continentale. Vous représenterez Oxfam au plus haut niveau auprès de l’UA, nouerez des relations stratégiques et contribuerez à positionner Oxfam comme un partenaire crédible et de confiance. Ce poste joue un rôle central dans la réalisation de la mission d’Oxfam en Afrique : il établit un lien entre les espaces d’élaboration des politiques continentales et les réalités nationales, tout en veillant à ce que les actions de plaidoyer soient cohérentes, porteuses d’impact et ancrées dans les réalités vécues par les communautés. Ce poste relève de la Direction Afrique, avec un rattachement matriciel à la Direction Plaidoyer, Campagnes et Engagement (ACE). Profil recherché Nous recherchons une personne reconnue pour son leadership en matière de plaidoyer et d’influence, disposant d’une solide expérience de collaboration avec l’Union africaine ou des institutions multilatérales comparables. Vous avez démontré votre capacité à concevoir et à mettre en œuvre des stratégies d’influence porteuses d’impact, combinant analyse des politiques, plaidoyer, communication médiatique et partenariats afin de favoriser des changements significatifs. Vous excellez dans l’établissement de relations et la négociation, savez évoluer efficacement dans des environnements complexes associant de multiples parties prenantes et êtes en mesure d’exercer une influence au plus haut niveau. Grâce à votre capacité de réflexion stratégique et d’analyse politique, vous savez traduire les processus de l’UA en possibilités concrètes d’influence et d’impact pour les pays et les partenaires. Votre expérience du leadership vous permet de diriger des équipes diversifiées et de travailler au sein d’un réseau mondial, tout en favorisant la collaboration et la redevabilité. Vous avez une connaissance approfondie du contexte sociopolitique africain et adhérez aux approches féministes, décoloniales et portées par les partenaires. La maîtrise professionnelle de l’anglais et du français est indispensable. Pourquoi nous rejoindre Ce poste offre une occasion rare d’influencer les politiques et les pratiques au plus haut niveau continental. À Oxfam, vous façonnerez notre engagement auprès de l’Union africaine, piloterez le plaidoyer sur des enjeux majeurs tels que les inégalités, la pauvreté et la justice, et collaborerez avec des gouvernements, des diplomates et des institutions internationales pour réaliser des changements concrets. Au sein d’une équipe de direction diversifiée et collaborative, vous contribuerez à rapprocher les politiques continentales des réalités des communautés, afin que les décisions prises au plus haut niveau se traduisent par des résultats tangibles pour les populations partout en Afrique. Ce que nous offrons À Oxfam, nous sommes convaincus que chaque aspect de notre travail peut contribuer à un changement positif. Si vous partagez cette conviction et possédez les compétences nécessaires pour relever les défis liés à ce poste, cette fonction vous offrira de grandes possibilités d’épanouissement personnel ainsi que d’excellentes perspectives d’évolution professionnelle. Oxfam s’engage à proposer une rémunération équitable, sur la base d’une semaine de travail de 36 heures À propos de nous Oxfam est un mouvement mondial de personnes qui agissent ensemble pour mettre fin à l’injustice qu’est la pauvreté. Cela signifie que nous nous attaquons aux inégalités qui maintiennent les populations dans la pauvreté. Ensemble, nous sauvons des vies, protégeons les populations et les aidons à reconstruire leur existence. Lorsqu’une catastrophe survient, nous aidons les personnes à bâtir un avenir meilleur, pour elles-mêmes et pour les autres. Nous agissons sur des enjeux tels que les droits fonciers, le changement climatique et les discriminations à l’égard des femmes. Et nous ne nous arrêterons pas tant que chaque personne sur la planète ne pourra pas vivre à l’abri de la pauvreté. Nous sommes une confédération internationale composée de 22 organisations affiliées et du Secrétariat d’Oxfam International. Avec nos partenaires et les communautés locales, nous menons des actions humanitaires, des programmes de développement et des campagnes dans plus de 76 pays. Oxfam en Afrique (OiA) est une plateforme continentale qui assure la coordination des bureaux pays d’Oxfam en Afrique et collabore avec des organisations de la société civile, des universitaires, des gouvernements et le secteur privé afin de contribuer à une Afrique plus égalitaire, en remettant en cause les structures de pouvoir qui perpétuent les inégalités et les injustices. À cette fin, Oxfam en Afrique apporte un leadership intellectuel dynamique et offre un espace de collaboration à ses partenaires. Oxfam en Afrique joue un rôle moteur dans l’appui aux communautés locales et le renforcement de leur pouvoir d’agir, la promotion de l’égalité de genre, le plaidoyer en faveur de changements de politiques publiques et le renforcement des capacités des organisations locales de la société civile. L’ensemble de notre travail est guidé par nos valeurs fondamentales : Autonomisation, Redevabilité, Inclusion, Courage, Solidarité et Égalité. Notre engagement en matière de safeguarding (Protection contre le harcèlement, l’exploitation et les abus sexuels) Oxfam s’engage à prévenir toute forme de comportement inapproprié au travail, notamment le harcèlement sexuel, l’exploitation et les abus sexuels, les manquements à l’intégrité et les irrégularités financières, ainsi qu’à promouvoir le bien-être des enfants, des jeunes et des adultes. Oxfam attend de l’ensemble de son personnel et de ses volontaires qu’ils partagent cet engagement et respectent notre Code de conduite. Nous accordons une importance primordiale au recrutement de personnes qui partagent nos valeurs et les mettent en pratique. Remarque : Toute offre d’emploi sera subordonnée à la réception de références satisfaisantes et pourra faire l’objet de contrôles appropriés, notamment une vérification du casier judiciaire et des contrôles relatifs au financement du terrorisme. Le Secrétariat d’Oxfam International participe également au Mécanisme interorganisations de divulgation des inconduites (Inter-Agency Misconduct Disclosure Scheme). Conformément à ce dispositif, si une personne candidate a précédemment travaillé pour une autre organisation membre, nous solliciterons auprès de cette organisation des informations concernant toute constatation d’exploitation sexuelle, d’abus sexuels et/ou de harcèlement sexuel survenue pendant son emploi, ainsi que tout incident qui faisait encore l’objet d’une enquête au moment de son départ. En soumettant sa candidature, la personne candidate confirme avoir pris connaissance de cette procédure de recrutement.

How to Apply: **Comment postuler** Si vous souhaitez influencer les politiques continentales et renforcer l’engagement auprès de l’Union africaine afin de favoriser des changements durables en Afrique, nous vous invitons à postuler. Veuillez soumettre un CV à jour et une lettre de motivation via ce lien [https://oxfam.current-vacancies.com/Jobs/Advert/4325897?cid=3360](https://oxfam.current-vacancies.com/Jobs/Advert/4325897?cid=3360) , en démontrant clairement en quoi votre profil répond aux critères essentiels définis dans la fiche de poste de Responsable du Bureau de plaidoyer et de liaison auprès de l’Union africaine. Veuillez noter que seules les personnes présélectionnées seront contactées, généralement dans les deux semaines suivant la date de clôture

title: Head of Network Development
description:
HEAD OF NETWORK DEVELOPMENT Location Global, whereHelpAge can currently employ: Ethiopia, India, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, Nepal, Pakistan, Spain, Tanzania, Thailand, Turkey, United Kingdom or Zimbabwe, with a preference for candidates based in the Global South. Department Network Development Reports to (Line Manager) Director of Global Impact Responsible for (Line managing) Regional Advisers (4) Network SupportLead Humanitarian Capacity Strengthening Manager ( SHAPE ) Network Platform Manager SCORE Programme Manager Indirectly responsible for Country Director – Ukraine (viathe Network Support Lead) Grade F Contract Type Full time equivalent /Open-ended contract About HelpAge HelpAge International works with a diverse global network of around 200 organisations across 99 countries to promote the rights of older people to lead dignified, healthy and secure lives. Through partnership and collaborations, we work to ensure the inclusion of older people across society and strive to deliver a just and fair world for everyone as they get older. Our work is driven by our desire to achieve real impact for older people, to be inclusive, to work in partnership and to learn from our shared experience. As countries prepare for and adapt to population ageing, we are seeking to make a difference at a critical juncture to how societies, economies and institutions adapt to this change. Our Strategy 2030, Ageing in a Just World, sets out how we will work to shape the future we all share. By working together with our partners, we aim to inspire a movement for change. By ensuring all our work promotes older people’s wellbeing, dignity and voice, we seek to transform the lives of older people now and in the future. Guided by our commitment to our values of impact, learning, partnership, and inclusion, we partner with others to bring systemic change and impact at scale. By acting as a supporter, convenor and thought leader, we want to make an impact that matters for older people and their communities. Our organisational culture The culture of the organisation aims to ensure: Accountability for All: Every individual and team member is responsible for their actions and decisions, ensuring alignment with organisational priorities and commitments to partners and network members. Trust, Respect, and Inclusion: We strive to create an environment where mutual trust is the foundation of all relationships, diverse perspectives are valued, and everyone feels included in decision-making processes. Culture of Collaboration: Working together across teams, network members, and partners to share knowledge, maximise impact, and drive collective success, rather than working in silos. Openness and Transparency: Ensuring open communication, clear decision-making processes and actions, and a commitment to sharing information in a way that builds trust and accountability. Collective Responsibilities Within and With Partners and Network: Recognising that achieving our mission requires shared responsibility, we promote joint ownership of decisions, initiatives, and outcomes across HelpAge and its network members and partners. Staff and network members are valued: Staff and network members are recognised, and valued and appreciated for their contributions, fostering an environment where every individual feels respected, supported, and integral to our mission, with their input and expertise recognised as vital to achieving our shared goals. The Behavioural competencies outlined below support this culture. About the Department The Global Impact Team drives HelpAge International’s mission to advance the wellbeing, dignity, and rights of older people, by championing locally led action and global solidarity. At the heart of our work is a thriving, resilient HelpAge global network—a powerful collective of national civil society actors driving change that is rooted in the priorities and experiences of older people. We lead the delivery of HelpAge’s strategic approach to support, convene, and influence, across humanitarian and development contexts, to achieve lasting and inclusive impact. Our goal is to ensure that: Older people have inclusive, improved access to secure and adequate income Older people have safe and secure access to humanitarian assistance Older people have improved access to inclusive health, care, and support services Age-inclusive laws, policies and systems guarantee older people’s rights across all sectors A thriving locally led HelpAge Network drives collective action to uphold older people’s rights, dignity, and wellbeing. About the Job The Head of Network Development will provide strategic leadership for HelpAge International's global network engagement and development, localisation, and capacity strengthening work - advancing our commitment to locally led action and building strong, values-driven relationships with network members and other strategic partners. This role will lead and be accountable for the development and delivery of the HelpAge network strategy, ensuring alignment with our global mission and enabling inclusive, sustainable collaboration across the HelpAge network. The postholder provides strategic leadership for network engagement, development and capacity strengthening across all regions - Africa, Asia, Eurasia and the Middle East, Europe, and Latin America and the Caribbean. They lead through the Regional Advisers rather than delivering regional workstreams personally: setting annual priorities and deliverables for each region, in alignment with organisational priorities, and hold Regional Advisers accountable for delivery through regular performance management and review. This is an evolving role. The postholder ensures the capacity strengthening and localisation offer is shaped by what members themselves identify as their needs and differentiated by region and member segment, rather than applied uniformly. title: Country Representative for Ethiopia, Based in Addis Ababa
description:
WHAT IS IMPACT INITIATIVES ? OUR AIM: IMPACT aims to shape practices and influence policies in humanitarian and development settings, in order to positively impact the lives of people and their communities. Created in 2010, IMPACT is a Geneva-based NGO and the largest independent data provider in contexts of crisis. We aim to support a range of stakeholders in making better, more informed decisions in humanitarian, stabilisation, and development settings. We believe that a key pathway to better planning and decision-making is direct engagement with local communities. HOW DO WE WORK ? IMPACT takes an initiative-based approach to structuring our programming. Each initiative has a specific aim, operational model, and portfolio of solutions. REACH strengthens evidence-based humanitarian decision-making through efficient data collection, management, and analysis - before, during, and after an emergency. PANDA improves the impact of humanitarian and development interventions through programme design, assessments, and monitoring & evaluation. AGORA promotes localised and multi-sectoral aid action in support of the recovery and stabilisation of crisis-affected communities, in partnership with local stakeholders Through our global team of research specialists, on average IMPACT publishes more than 1,700 information products on a yearly basis. In 2010, IMPACT was launched at the initiative of ACTED, an international NGO whose headquarters are based in Paris and is present in thirty countries. The two organizations have a strong complementarity formalized in a global partnership, which particularly allows IMPACT to benefit from ACTED’s operational support in its fields of intervention. We are currently looking for a Country Representative to lead our Ethiopia mission, based in Addis Abeba Position: Country Representative Contract duration: 12 months Location: Addis Abeba, Ethiopia, with potential travel to Kampala, Uganda Starting Date: October / November 2026 Application Deadline: 09 October 2026. COUNTRY PROFILE Since 2018, Ethiopia has experienced escalating insecurity and unrest, including large-scale displacement, loss of life, and widespread destruction of property, following significant domestic political changes. These crises have compounded the effects of recurring climate-related shocks affecting large parts of the country. In November 2020, conflict erupted in the northern Tigray region, triggering significant displacement across Tigray, Amhara, and Afar regions. Since August 2023, renewed conflict in Amhara has further intensified humanitarian needs, leading to the declaration of a state of emergency and restrictions on movement across the region. Together, these crises have severely disrupted livelihoods, constrained access to essential goods and staple commodities, and increased the vulnerability of affected populations, placing additional pressure on humanitarian response capacities across the country. FUNCTIONS Under the management of IMPACT’s Regional Coordinator (RC) for Africa in Geneva, the Country Representative (CR) is responsible for representing IMPACT and managing and developing IMPACT’s programmes in Ethiopia. S/he leads the IMPACT team to achieve program excellence and ensure the highest level of impact and accountability, while ensuring compliance to IMPACT guidelines, policies and standards across the mission. The CR is in regular contact with HQ, ensuring that organizational risks are promptly and clearly communicated to the Regional Coordinator and other relevant HQ Senior Management. S/he will promote organizational vision and core values across the mission and will actively link with HQ to contribute to the implementation of IMPACT’s global strategy. In his/her mission, the Country Representative will be hosted by Acted and will fall under the direct responsibility and management of Acted’s Country Director for all Administrative, Security, Logistics and Finance issues. S/he will therefore fully abide by Acted’s Security, HR, Administration and Logistics rules and regulations, and, in coordination with Acted, will ensure that all IMPACT staff abide by them. RESPONSIBILITIES The Country Representative responsibilities include the following: Strategic Leadership Develop and execute an up-to-date Country Strategy aligned with IMPACT’s global objectives and Ethiopia’s humanitarian landscape. Identify strategic opportunities, consolidate ongoing initiatives, and explore new programme areas to enhance IMPACT’s value to the aid community. Programme and Project Management In coordination with the Deputy Country Representative, oversee programme planning, implementation, and evaluation, ensuring all projects meet objectives, timelines, and compliance standards. Facilitate coordination between IMPACT and partner organizations to achieve efficient project delivery and impact. Fundraising and Donor Engagement Identify and secure funding opportunities in collaboration with HQ and Acted. Lead proposal development and negotiate contracts with donors, ensuring alignment with strategic priorities. Operations Support the Operations Managers and Project Development and Partnership Officers in building and maintaining a broad network of partner organizations to strengthen operational capacity and facilitate the implementation of activities in hard-to-reach and underserved areas. Continue to explore alternative operational models and innovative research approaches to expand geographic and population coverage, particularly among marginalized and difficult-to-reach communities. Ensure regular coordination with Acted's project development and FLATS departments (finance, logistics, administration, transparency, security) at all stages of project development and implementation. Finance and Budget Oversight Manage project budgets and forecast expenses, ensuring accurate and timely financial reporting to HQ and Acted. Mitigate financial risks and ensure optimal budget utilization. Human Resources and Team Leadership In consultation with the Deputy Country Representative, guide and develop the IMPACT team, ensuring performance standards, capacity building, and adherence to IMPACT and Acted’s policies. Coordinate with HQ and Acted for transparent recruitment and career management of staff. External Representation and Coordination Establish and maintain productive relationships with donors, UN agencies, NGOs, and other stakeholders, representing IMPACT’s programmes and strategic interests. Ensure proactive contribution to key humanitarian decision-making forums and promote IMPACT’s programme visibility. Data Protection and Accountability Uphold strict confidentiality of all data collected and engage with communities respectfully, ensuring awareness of programme objectives and methods. REQUIREMENTS Academic qualifications: Excellent academic qualifications, including a Master’s degree in a relevant discipline (International Relations, Political Sciences, Social Research, Development Studies, or similar). Management experience: Previous experience in a senior management role in an INGO at field level. Track record in successful management of international and national teams in humanitarian contexts. Familiarity with aid system: Familiarity with the aid system, and the research community. Communication/reporting skills: Excellent communication and drafting skills for effective reporting, including proven experience in contributing to high level presentations/briefings. Years of work experience: At least 5 years of relevant working experience. Any previous experience in Ethiopia would be an asset. Research skills: Experience in assessments. M&E, field research, evaluations an asset. Multi-tasking skills: Ability to multitask with tight deadlines in complex environment. Level of independence: A self-starter with a proven ability to work independently. Cross-cultural work environment: Ability to operate in a cross-cultural environment. Language skills: Fluency in English required**.** Security environment: Ability to operate in a complex and challenging security environment. COMPENSATION AND BENEFITS For this position, salary between 4’050€ and 4’100€ monthly (before income tax), etc as well as a monthly living allowance of 500 USD NB - IMPACT salaries are strictly determined by our salary grid depending on the grade of the position and the level of education of staff. title: Consultant - Final Evaluation Coherence programme Ethiopia
description:
1. Introduction The COHERENCE programme Ethiopia 2022-2026 is implemented by Ethiopian Catholic Church – Social and Development Commission Soddo branch (ECC-SDCO/S) and Adigrat branch (ECC-SDCO/Ad) , with coordination support by the East Africa regional programme Manager CI.be. The programme is implemented in 7 countries and is co-funded by the Belgian Government. The program’s aim is to equip rural communities so that they become more resilient and can better cope with crisis situations. Above all, the program wants the most vulnerable people, particularly women, young people and people with disabilities, to have expanded opportunities to improve their living conditions. Through a ‘triple nexus ’ approach, focus is on (1) social cohesion, peace-building and rights protection within communities; (2) rural economic development; and (3) disaster preparedness The present terms of reference relate exclusively to the final evaluation of COHERENCE Ethiopia. The final evaluations of the three other country programs are the subject of separate tenders and fall outside the scope of this assignment. 2. Object of the evaluation: COHERENCE Ethiopia 2.1 Program objective, results and activities To address food insecurity of poor and vulnerable households – with a focus on female-headed and landless households – of 2 kebeles in Damot Woyde district (Wolaita) and 2 kebeles in Irob district (Eastern Tigray) , COHERENCE Ethiopia aimed to improve their livelihood base in a sustainable way, by means of a triple nexus approach, linking three complementary areas: social cohesion, rural economic development and disaster risk reduction (DRR). The action’s specific objective was formulated as follows: “By the end of 2026, poor and vulnerable households, especially resource poor female-headed and landless households, in two kebeles (Endamosa and Hareze Sabata) of Irob district and two kebeles (Kindo Koyo and Mayo Kote) of Damot Woyde district have strengthened their livelihood basis, better enabling them to seize opportunities and realize their aspirations”. The objective was to be achieved through three results. A first result concerned social cohesion that was to be improved by building household and community capacity to manage resource-induced conflicts and to ensure equitable and fair access or entitlement to natural resources, through, among others: Conducting a rapid gender context analysis at community level (1 in each intervention area); Organizing in groups and training of 180 community cohesion and gender empowerment agents on peace building, conflict management and facilitation skills; Organizing community dialogue sessions on peace and conflict management and gender equity (while applying the household transformation method); Rehabilitating and expanding water piping to address existing water access conflict (Wolaita); Planting tree seedlings on communal land between communities as a joint, social cohesion enhancing activity (Tigray); Providing energy-saving stoves for 300 households (Wolaita). The direct causes of food insecurity in the intervention zones are – besides the two-year war in Tigray (2020-2022) – the depletion of household assets and continuous dwindling of income. Repeated food shortages have also forced many households to sell their assets to address immediate needs. Therefore, through a second result , the program aimed to contribute to improving household production, income, savings and productive assets by: Supporting households in income generating activities and household asset building; Organizing, training and equipping savings and and internal lending groups (SILCs) to enhance solidarity, savings and resilience; Selecting specific Household Asset Building Packages (HABP), providing technical and basic business training of HABP-SILC groups, and supporting households in financing business plans by means of subsidy. Finally, a third result sought to strengthen vulnerable households' resilience in response to climate-induced shocks and stress, by focusing on improving farm production by: Organizing volunteer smallholders in “community learning groups” (type of farmer field schools) and providing orientation training on Resilience Design (RD); Facilitating self-assessments based on local knowledge, practices and exchange; Increasing soil fertility with appropriate durable techniques identified using a RD approach; Supplying farm-resilient seeds and biological catalysator (for compost making) (Tigray); Providing energy-saving tools for households with special needs; Conducting quality monitoring and group learning of RD-related activities implemented at farm-level through community learning groups or famer field school groups. In addition, by means of workshops, exchange visits, networking and inclusive and participatory MEAL, stakeholders were expected to mutually reinforce each other's capacities, in particular with regard to issues addressed by the program. 2.2 Target groups COHERENCE Ethiopia’s implementation period extended over 42 and 36 months respectively in Wolaita and Eastern Tigray, addressing a total of at least 1,900 households (1,000 in Wolaita and 900 in Eastern Tigray). More specifically, the program targeted: With regard to social cohesion: 1,900 households (1,000 in Wolaita, 900 in Tigray) of which 1,327 are male-headed (787 in Wolaita, 540 in Tigray) and 573 female-headed (213 in Wolaita, 360 in Tigray), 4 peace and social cohesion and gender equity promoting groups, and 180 peace and social cohesion agents / community leaders (elders, religious leaders, women and youth representatives, …) (75 in Wolaita, 105 in Tigray); With regard to rural economic development (household asset building): 830 poor households (400 in Wolaita, 430 in Tigray) with priority for female-headed and landless households, and 49 SILCs (20 in Wolaita, 29 in Tigray); With regard to disaster risk reduction (resilience design): 800 smallholder households (600 in Wolaita, 200 in Tigray), with a priority for smallholders vulnerable to climate change; Government technical staff. In addition to these target-groups, i.e. direct beneficiaries, the following indirect beneficiaries were foreseen: The population of the 2 kebeles (Endamosa and Hareze Sabata) in Eastern Tigray and of the 2 kebeles (Kindo Koyo and Mayo Kote) in Wolaita; Government services and local authorities of the 4 kebeles; Authorities of Irob and Damot Woyde districts. 2.3 Three innovative approaches Three approaches are assumed to have particularly contributed to the action’s achievements and are to receive specific attention during the final evaluation (see evaluation questions below). 2.3.1 Social cohesion and peace building through village peace agents To encourage peace building and social cohesion, COHERENCE Ethiopia mobilized volunteers from the targeted communities who were expected to become “change agents”.They were trained on basic peace building and conflict management and thus equipped with knowledge and skills on grassroots conflict prevention, management and resolution. Thereto, the program adopted the so-called the 3Bs/4Ds methodology (cf. https://ics.crs.org/resource/ties-bind-building-social-cohesion-divided-communities ) that combines binding, bonding and bridging (the 3Bs) with appreciative inquiry (the 4Ds: discover, dream, design and deliver) to enable communities to cooperate and collaborate across ethnic, religious, gender, class and other divides and to strengthen horizontal and vertical rights relations and social cohesion. Following this methodology, key grassroots actors were accompanied in discovering their individual and collective strengths and their mutual responsibilities in promoting social cohesion. At the heart of the methodology is a focus on what connects and energizes people, rather than on obstacles and issues that separate them. The trained change agents were to facilitate “community dialogues sessions” that focused on tensions and conflicts that had been identified through a rapid conflict analysis and a limited social cohesion barometer survey. 2.3.2 Gender empowerment Apart from promoting peace and social cohesion, the community volunteers were also expected to be change agents with regard to gender relations in their community. They were trained on gender analysis and participatory gender transformative methods and tools. A rapid gender context analysis was conducted and based on its findings, gender transformation activities were engaged in by the program at two levels. First, at village level, trained change agents organized, in collaboration with the program’s community animators, community conversation sessions on gender issues with groups of men and women, giving participants room to talk, discuss and exchange ideas about gender perceptions and roles in their households and at community level. Next, using two complementary gender transformation methods (the Household Transformation Method (HTM) and Gender Action Learning (GAL) ), male and female members of households were supported in assessing and analyzing intra-household gender disparities (division of labor, access to and control of household resources, benefits sharing mechanisms, decision-making power, etc.). Ultimately, the approach was to result in bringing about change and improvement in terms of the gender empowerment index. 2.3.3 Community Learning Groups Co-creation and sharing of knowledge plays a central role in the process of developing and implementing agroecological innovations including climate change adaptation. To create together and share knowledge, farmers need a platform that supports them to work in small groups and have opportunities to articulate ideas, increase their motivation and participation to innovate and adapt, build trust and collaborate among themselves and with other stakeholders (e.g. extension workers) and strengthen effective linkages with stakeholders. One way in which co-creation and knowledge sharing can be encouraged is by establishing and strengthening Community Learning Groups (CLG) at grassroots. While in other approaches Farmer Field Schools (FFS) or Farmer Training Centers (FTC) are used as centers where people go and learn or acquire knowledge, a CLG is a group of active and interested individual farmers organized for peer-to-peer learning and experience or knowledge sharing, regardless of age, sex and social group. Most of the time, experience sharing and visiting events take place among members and external experts and trainers are invited on demand only. Farmers participating in the Ethiopia program thus established such CLGs. While participating in these groups, they implemented resilience design activities concerning soil health, soil and water conservation and crop diversification. Group membership is based on proximity of farmland. The program strengthened the CLGs’ capacity by means of an orientation session and training on the CLG approach and its objectives and its added value compared with other extension approaches. With the support of the program, the CLGs established bylaws and appointed their leadership (chairperson, secretary and record keeper). They meet once per month to share experiences and to learn. For each meeting the agenda – including issues for discussion, whether or not to invite external persons, etc. – is set by the CLG leaders in consultation with members. The CLG members visit each other’s farm, possibly accompanied by a development agent (DA), to see and exchange on and learn from the resilience design activities that were accomplished at the farm. The CLG approach was expected to encourage dissemination of good practices within and outside communities. Within a community, larger CLGs could be divided into smaller ones at village-level or below, so that the number of people participating in experience exchange could be multiplied. The budget of COHERENCE Ethiopia is 849,799 Euro. 3. Purpose and objectives of the evaluation The final evaluation of the COHERENCE Ethiopia program aims at: Identifying lessons learned in the introduction and adoption of social methodological innovation in view of future programming by CI.be and its partners; Ensuring accountability towards donors and other stakeholders , by rendering public the results of program performance assessment. These two objectives will be accomplished by answering three evaluation questions concerning the implementation of the three methodological approaches – presented above in § 2.3. – within the overall HDP nexus perspective. These approaches – respectively involving village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups – are considered innovative and key to the achievement of the program’s outcome. The intended users of the final evaluation’s results include the following: Implementation and coordination teams of partners ECC-SDCO/Ad and ECC-SDCO/S; CI.be staff at regional offices and head office and partner staff involved in joint development programming; Staff of other development actors (through publication of the final evaluation report on the CI.be website); DGD, the program donor (accountability). 4. Scope of the evaluation, evaluation criteria and evaluation questions With regard to its scope, the final evaluation will cover the COHERENCE Ethiopia program in both intervention areas, that is, in both Wolaita and Eastern Tigray, although – given the uncertain security situation in Tigray – fieldwork is expected to be restricted to solely Wolaita. Focus will be on the performance of three innovative methodological approaches, implemented by the program within a nexus approach: village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups. The DAC criteria that will be taken into account include coherence , effectiveness and sustainability . In addition, particular attention will be paid to the performance of the intervention in terms of inclusiveness in the fight against poverty and organisational strengthening of the target groups. The following evaluation questions are proposed (to be refined and prioritised during the framing phase): To what extent was the nexus approach adopted by the program appropriate and adequate foraddressing the target groups’ priority needs? [DAC criteria: coherence and sustainability] To what extent were the pathways of change and assumptions (theory of change) and the intervention logic (results framework) coherent, plausible and feasible? To what extent were the three innovative approaches (village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups) critical in the adopted design of the nexus approach? To what extent did they contribute to integrating the three pillars of the nexus (synergies between the pillars)? To what extent did the innovations fall short in reaching the different vulnerable groups targeted by the program (LNOB)? What have been the roles and contributions of the three innovative approaches (village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups) in achieving program outcomes ? [DAC criteria: effectiveness and sustainability] To what extent and how have the three innovative approaches beeneffective in bringing about behavioral change and adoption of new practices at target group level? Which are the factors that were conducive to these changes ? Which factors can be identified that have hindered or slowed down changes? To what extent did the 3 methods function better than other existing alternative methods in achieving program outcomes? To what extent and how are the three innovative approaches transformative? Can we see early signs of enduring changes in norms and systems ? To what extent has the program created enabling mechanisms to sustain the positive effects induced by the three innovative approaches?[DAC criteria: coherence and sustainability] How appropriate was the process of introducing the three innovative approaches within the targeted communities? Did the program learn from and adapt these innovative approaches or other activities during their implementation? What was the contribution of the MEAL process in this? To what extent do the stakeholders of the intervention – including government actiors and target groups – take ownership of the results achieved by means of the three innovative approaches and how committed are they to sustaining these results after the program’s closure? To what extent has the program built capacities of key stakeholders (implementing partners, government sector offices and target groups) required to institutionalize the innovative approaches without forsaking grassroots ownership and leadership and allowing continued flow of benefits? For each evaluation question clear and relevant lessons on introducing innovations are to be identified for use in the formulation and implementation of future programs and projects, in terms of: Operationalizing the nexus; Achieving program outputs and outcomes; Sustaining outcomes and institutionalizing approaches. 5. Approach and methodology The evaluator's offer in response to this tender should include, as part of the technical offer, a methodological proposal that shows how the evaluator will proceed to achieve the evaluation’s objectives, to make the evaluation useful and to present results that meet high quality standards. The evaluator will favour participatory methods wherever possible. The teams in Ethiopia suggest a combination of a theory-based approach (using comparative case studies) and outcome harvesting. The methodological proposal will contain : A preliminary evaluability assessment , which should demonstrate the main conditions and limitations that the evaluation will face in achieving the planned objectives and in finding answers to the questions posed. It will also indicate how evaluability problems can be solved; The general theoretical-methodological approach that will guide the final evaluation ; A proposal for accompanying the documentation process (case studies) that the project teams will engage in themselves in complement to the final evaluation and for integrating that documentation in the approach and conduct of the final evaluation itself; A proposal for an analytical framework/evaluation matrix for the external evaluation, including evaluation questions, evaluation criteria, means, and sources of information. This matrix is a tool for the implementation of the evaluation questions, but does not replace the theoretical-methodological approach that will guide the evaluation and that should be presented in a clear and differentiated way in the proposal; A description of the evaluation techniques and tools that will be used to collect, classify, analyse and present the required data . The use and analysis of existing and accessible quantitative data is expected. The use of quantitative methods requiring the collection of primary data by the evaluator is not requested. The following sources of information will be made available to the evaluator (list not exhaustive): The theory of change and the program proposal including the results framework; Baseline survey report; Internal narrative annual reports, performance scores and lessons learned (2023-2025, and draft documents for 2026); Monitoring data collected and reports produced by the implementing partners; Resource persons at the level of CI.be and implementing partners. Other documents can be provided upon the evaluator’s request (e.g. concerning meetings, trainings, etc., organised within the framework of the program). 6. Coordination of the evaluation The final evaluation will be coordinated by CI.be’s regional program manager based in Addis Ababa and Ethiopia desk in Brussels, with the support of CI.be’s MEAL officer. The regional program manager and desk officer will be first points of contact of the evaluator, with whom meetings will take place at least at certain specific moments of the process: initial briefing, finalisation of the terms of reference and framing note, discussion of the detailed methodological approach, etc. The regional program manager and desk officer will be responsible for monitoring, accompanying and facilitating the final evaluation process, and more concretely for: Facilitating the evaluator’s access to relevant sources of information (documentation, data, people); Facilitating communication between the evaluator, program implementation teams and partners, and other stakeholders; Monitoring and quality assurance of the process. The formulation of these terms of reference relied on an ongoing consultative process with the implementing partners ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad throughout the program. They will also be consulted during the final evaluation at appropriate times (framing note, draft evaluation report, etc.). Logistics of the evaluation will be coordinated by the regional program manager and ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad. 7. Reports and feedback Nature of the documents to be delivered According to a timetable agreed at the start of the evaluation and in accordance with § 8.2, the evaluator will provide the following documents and reports: A methodological “framing note” specifying the approach and methods that will be used by the evaluator to collect the required data and information; A provisional evaluation report presented for discussion and comment to CI.be and the implementing partners; A final evaluation report taking into account the remarks made on the provisional report and/or adding in annex the collection of comments not taken into account, accompanied by the reasons for not doing so. Quality of the documents Reports should be understandable and easy to read. The results and analyses must be detailed. Causal links between findings, conclusions and recommendations should be clearly visible and sequences of reasoning clearly expressed. Conclusions and recommendations should be well argued and usable in an optimal way by the final evaluation’s stakeholders (CI.be and partners, DGD, other stakeholders, ...). It is therefore important that the recommendations are limited in number number and presented in order of priority and that they are operational in order to facilitate CI.be’s and partners’ management responses. Where relevant, different options available can be explored as well as risks and limitations associated with each option. Structure of the final report Table of contents ; List of abbreviations and acronyms; Executive summary (maximum 1 page, including main findings and recommendations, with interpretation); Key information on the program and the methodology used; Well-argued findings on the evaluation questions and DAC criteria (analysing the collected and accessed data); Conclusions and recommendations, including a synthetic table presenting findings – recommendations – targeted actor (maximum 4 pages); Annexes: Terms of Reference; implemented work program (activities, list of people and organizations met, …); list of documentation consulted; inventory and documentation of lessons learned; comments not taken into account, with reasons for not taking them into account. Even though the inventory and documentation of lessons learned is presented in an annex, it should be treated as of equal importance to the main report. 8. Practical aspects 8.1 The process Phase 1: framing the assignment The evaluator will finalise the methodological approach proposed in their offer on the basis of initial briefings by CI.be and a first reading of the documents (as mentioned in § 5) shared with them. The documentation will be made available to the evaluator at the start of their work. This stage will be an opportunity for the evaluator and CI.be and its partners to conclude possible refining of the evaluation questions presented in § 4. Phase 2: documentation through case studies The partners and implementation teams in Eastern Tigray and Wolaita can engage in case studies, intended to complement the documentation process and to support the external evaluation. CI.be encourages that such case studies are organized, while being accompanied methodologically by the evaluator, who then monitors and validates the process and its relevance for the final evaluation. Phase 3: desk study and preparation of field visit During this phase, the main stakeholders involved in the field visit will be identified. The evaluator will interview online or in-person key staff of CI.be at head office and regional office, read the available documentation and develop a methodological approach (including a timetable, persons and/or groups to be met and organisation of first local feedback meeting/workshop). Phase 4: field visit The fieldwork will concern only the action in Wolaita, given the uncertain security situation in Eastern Tigray. Primary data collection will take into account budget constraints as well as the existence of particular implementation problems, etc. It will focus on those locations and key persons that are considered most relevant in assessing the three methodological innovations in the nexus approach. Sufficient time needs to be planned for methodological briefing and participatory analysis involving the implementation team and stakeholders in Wolaita. The field visit should enable triangulation of the information obtained from the reading and analysis of the documentation of the action with primary data and participatory analysis and sense making with the program teams of the two partner organizations and CI.be’s regional program manager. To allow the Eastern Tigray project team’s involvement in this sense making, they will be invited to participate in the feedback workshop to be organized in Wolaita (to the extent that the budget allows). Phase 5 : data analysis, reporting, presentation and feedback The evaluator will analyse the collected data and produce a draft report, to be presented and discussed at an online feedback session, in which CI.be, ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad will participate. Taking into account these discussions, the evaluator will finalise the evaluation report. S/he will be free to take the comments into consideration or not. However, the remarks which s/he does not take into account must be included in an annex, together with the justification for not taking them into account. In addition, the evaluator is expected to present and participate in an online sensemaking meeting with the program teams of all 7 country programs. The evaluation plan calls for findings and relevant actions to be shared and analysed among country program teams in order to be appropriately leveraged and ensure a collective, horizontal learning process. 8.2 Available budget COHERENCE Ethiopia has foreseen a budget of € 15,000 for its final evaluation, which the offer should not exceed. The amount is understood to be exclusive of expenses related to mobilization of target groups, fieldwork logistics, etc. Otherwise, the tender must include all costs associated with carrying out the assignment: fees, travel expenses, daily allowances, insurance, reproduction costs and any other expenses. The financial offer is deemed to be firm and final. The successful contractor must include in their tender a detailed work plan setting out the number of days worked per activity and per member of the evaluation team, as well as indicative dates and locations. This work plan will be discussed and approved as part of the methodological framing note. The payment terms are as follows: 30 per cent on signing the contract, 40 per cent upon submission of the draft report, and 30 per cent upon approval of the final report. 8.3 Calendar Indicative calendar: Tender: 09/2026 Analysis of offers: 09/2026 Decision on contract: 10/2026 Briefing: 10/2026 Methodological framing note: 10/2026 Documentation process by partners: 10/2026 - 11/2026 Desk study: 10/2026 - 11/2026 Field visit :11/2026 - 12/2026 Draft reporting and feedback: 12/2026 - 01/2027 Final report: 01/2027 Management response: 01/2027 Sharing of report: 02/2027 Multi-country sense making meeting: 12/2026 - 01/2027 8.4 Profile of the evaluator The evaluation should preferably be carried out by a mixed team of consultants. CI.be encourages gender balance among applicants. Required expertise and experience: Program design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, including outcome harvesting; Organisation of participatory evaluations; Capacity building of grassroots institutions and empowerment; Technical expertise areas: HDP nexus and conflict-sensitive development; Gender equity and empowerment; Agroecology; Social cohesion and peacebuilding (small p); Rural development and social technology innovation; Proficiency in "results-based management" and "theory of change" methods; Geographical experience in Ethiopia and knowledge of the local context (Wolaita, Eastern Tigray); Knowledge of local languages. The CVs of the evaluator and their team proposed for this evaluation must be attached to the technical and financial offer. 8.5 Selection of the evaluator Tenders will be evaluated on the basis of the quality of the technical offer (80%) and the price of the services offered (20%). The technical offer will be evaluated on the basis of: The methodological approach and understanding of the terms of reference; The proposed approach to the practical organisation of the evaluation (indicative timetable of the different phases); The qualifications and experience in the different fields mentioned above of the expert and team members proposed for the evaluation. For the technical offer, the tenderer must obtain 60% of the points relating to this criterion. If not, the bid will be disregarded. The financial offer (20%) will be evaluated on the basis of: The overall package price (10%); the score (NPX) for the price of offer X will be calculated as follows: NPX = 10 x (lowest bid price)/(bid price X); The average price for a day's service (10%); the score (NPMX) for the average price for a day's service of offer X will be calculated as follows: NPMX = 10 x (lowest average price)/(average price of offer X). The average price per day of service will be calculated by dividing the sum of salary/per diem/accommodation for the evaluation team by the number of days of service offered. All bidders commit to not having any conflict of interest in relation to the program to be evaluated, including in its preparatory phases. 9. Transparency, confidentiality, ethical standards and data ownership 9.1 Transparency and confidentiality The reports to be published will not contain any information that could endanger partners, teams or any other stakeholder, compromise the integrity of the program in any way, or pose any other risk in terms of confidentiality, particularly with regard to the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. The evaluator is required to respect the confidential nature of all documents and data to which they have access during the evaluation process. The results of the evaluation are intended to be made public, in the interest of accountability to the donor and external stakeholders. 9.2 Ethics The evaluator carries out their work in accordance with the quality standards and ethical principles customary in the evaluation sector, including independence of judgement, impartiality, transparency of methods, reporting of findings to those concerned, and respect for the dignity of the people interviewed. The free and informed consent of interviewees is obtained prior to any interview or focus group discussion. Participants are informed of the purpose of the evaluation, how their comments will be used, and their right to refuse answering or to withdraw at any time. Comments reported in the final report are anonymised, unless the persons concerned have given their explicit written consent. Particular attention is paid to the protection of vulnerable individuals. The evaluation team shall immediately report to CI.be any situation brought to its attention that could constitute a breach of personal integrity. 9.3 Conflict of interest Candidates shall declare, in their tender, that there is no conflict of interest, whether actual or apparent, with CI.be, ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad or the donor. In particular, a conflict of interest is deemed to exist where a person has designed, implemented or evaluated all or part of the intervention that is the subject of this evaluation, or where they have a contractual, financial or personal relationship that could compromise the independence of their judgement. Any conflict of interest arising in the course of the assignment must be reported without delay. The concealment of a conflict of interest constitutes grounds for termination of the contract. 9.4 Ownership and retention of data All data collected, transcripts, recordings, field notes, databases and deliverables produced in the course of the assignment are the exclusive property of Caritas International. The evaluator may not publish, disseminate or reuse all or part of these materials for any other purpose, nor transfer them to third parties, without prior written authorisation of the commissioning bodies. Personal data shall be processed in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation, stored securely for the duration of the assignment and destroyed, or handed over to the commissioning parties, no later than 1 month after the final report has been approved. A certificate of destruction shall be provided.

How to Apply: Interested candidates are invited to submit a technical proposal and a financial proposal. Proposals must not exceed 10 pages, excluding any attached CVs. The **technical proposal** shall include: • A methodological proposal; • A detailed work plan; • The CVs of the proposed team members, together with a breakdown of roles and responsibilities; • Professional references and an example of a relevant previous evaluation work; • A sworn statement confirming the absence of any conflict of interest. The **financial proposal**, quoted in euros, shall be broken down by type of cost and by man-day. It is to be a firm quote, inclusive of tax, and shall include all costs relating to the service. Offers must be sent by 30 September 2026 to Dorry Hagos (d.hagos@caritasint.be), with copies to Mark Breusers (m.breusers@caritasint.be) and Jozef Serneels (j.serneels@caritasint.be). If you have any questions or requests for information regarding this call for offers, please contact d.hagos@caritasint.be and/or m.breusers@caritasint.be.

title: Senior Portfolio Manager, NTDs
description:
About CBM CBM (registered as CBM Christoffel-Blindenmission Christian Blind Mission e.V.) is an international development organisation committed to improving the quality of life of persons with disabilities in the persons communities of the world. Based on our Christian values and more than 100 years of professional expertise, we address poverty as a cause and a consequence of disability. We work in partnership to create an inclusive society for all. About the role: We are looking for an experienced Senior Portfolio Manager to provide strategic leadership and oversight across CBM’s multi-country NTD donor portfolio. In this senior role, you will work across country programmes and global teams to strengthen portfolio performance, ensure effective grant management and donor compliance, oversee financial and operational risk, and build strong relationships with institutional donors and partners. You will provide strategic insight to inform decision-making, strengthen ways of working across the portfolio, and contribute to the continued growth and effectiveness of CBM’s NTD programmes. This position is only filled locally in one of CBM permanent established entities. (ex: Berlin or Bensheim (Germany), UK (Cambridge or remote), the US (remote), Nairobi (Kenya), Abuja (Nigeria), Lomé (Togo), Yaoundé (Cameroon), Lusaka (Zambia), Addis Abeba (Ethiopia), Guatemala City, Kampala (Uganda), Niamey (Niger), etc.). Local contractual conditions of the respective country will apply. An expatriation is not intended You Will: Lead grant management and donor compliance across CBM’s multi-country NTD donor portfolio, including quality assurance and compliance review of budgets, workplans, procurement plans and donor reports prior to submission. Oversee sub-award management, portfolio-wide compliance monitoring and donor reporting, identifying, mitigating and escalating compliance risks and promoting consistent grant management practices. Monitor portfolio performance, budget utilisation and delivery against agreed milestones, leading portfolio-level financial oversight and risk management. Identify and mitigate operational and compliance risks, providing strategic analysis and recommendations to support decision-making and portfolio effectiveness. Manage donor relationships and serve as a key programmatic interface with institutional donors and donor secretariats. Contribute to donor stewardship, resource mobilisation, business development and partnership opportunities, providing programme performance, compliance and impact information to support donor engagement. Coordinate grant compliance and portfolio management across country teams and relevant CBM functions, working with internal stakeholders to strengthen CBM’s position as a trusted and high-performing partner. Provide strategic and operational support to country programmes, with an initial focus on the RLMF portfolio while also supporting the wider NTD donor portfolio, particularly during critical planning, implementation and reporting periods. Capture and share lessons learned, facilitating collaboration, knowledge sharing and continuous improvement across the NTD portfolio. You Have: A relevant academic degree in international development, public health or a related field. Substantial experience in grants management within multi-country, donor-funded health or development programmes, including compliance monitoring, budgeting and sub-award management. Experience managing or advising on institutional donor compliance frameworks at portfolio or multi-country level. Strong working knowledge of the NTD landscape and major NTD/global health donors. Experience managing sub-award or sub-grant agreements with in-country partners. Experience working across multiple country offices in matrix or international environments. Strong donor-facing communication skills and the ability to engage effectively with senior stakeholders. Excellent organisational, analytical and cross-cultural relationship-building skills, with the ability to manage multiple priorities and deadlines with a high degree of autonomy. Professional proficiency in both English and French. Willingness to travel internationally and work flexibly across time zones. Identification with the Christian values and mandate of CBM. What we offer A meaningful position with a lot of creative freedom in the world's leading organisation in the field of Disability Inclusive Development A fair salary and other social benefits based on the local conditions in the country you apply for An approachable, agile organisation with self-reliant people in a diverse and collegial team and great team spirit

How to Apply: Please apply exclusively online via our applicant portal (see [APPLY NOW](https://jobs.cbm.org/Senior-Portfolio-Manager-NTDs-eng-f1091.html)). A letter of motivation, CV and relevant (work) references complete your application. We look forward to receiving your application! Your contact person: Ms. Eve Muthama We would like to further promote diversity in our teams and therefore welcome applications from people of different ethnic and social backgrounds, religions and world views, different ages and genders, and especially from people with disabilities. *Suitability is decisive, gender is irrelevant!*

Terms of Reference for IUCN Consultancy Title: Provision of Vehicle Rental Services Objective of the Consultancy This consultancy has the following objective: 1. To secure reliable transportation services for staff coordinating and supporting the implementation of the NbS4Water Africa – Ethiopia Awash Project Background Project Reference: - Donor reference: DN01983 About IUCN IUCN is a membership Union uniquely composed of both government and civil society organisations. It provides public, private and non-governmental organisations with the knowledge and tools that enable human progress, economic development and nature conservation to take place together. Created in 1948, IUCN is now the world’s largest and most diverse environmental network, harnessing the knowledge, resources and reach of more than 1,400 Member organisations and around 15,000 experts. It is a leading provider of conservation data, assessments and analysis. Its broad membership enables IUCN to fill the role of incubator and trusted repository of best practices, tools and international standards. IUCN provides a neutral space in which diverse stakeholders including governments, NGOs, scientists, businesses, local communities, indigenous peoples organisations and others can work together to forge and implement solutions to environmental challenges and achieve sustainable development. Working with many partners and supporters, IUCN implements a large and diverse portfolio of conservation projects worldwide. Combining the latest science with the traditional knowledge of local communities, these projects work to reverse habitat loss, restore ecosystems and improve people’s well-being. www.iucn.org https://twitter.com/IUCN/ About the Project The project focuses on promoting catchment protection through Nature-based Solutions (NbS), framed as best adaptive practices in the context of climate change and increasing land degradation. It aims to scale up NbS for watershed restoration in alignment with national basin development, land degradation neutrality, and landscape restoration goals. The general objective is to enhance water-related ecosystem services in key watersheds of the Awash sub-basin for the benefit of both people and the environment through the application of NbS. To achieve this, the project will strengthen action-oriented partnerships among community-based organizations (CBOs), the wider public, national and local governments, and non-government actors. These partnerships will promote NbS that build knowledge, shape positive attitudes, and encourage good practices, mobilizing society as a whole to achieve large-scale watershed rehabilitation, restoration, and sustainable development and use. The general objective of the project is to improve ground water recharge of the little Akaki catchment of the upper Awash river basin focusing on Guleel & Addis Ketema sub-cities of Addis Ababa and Sululta town of Sheger city, specifically in Bilisuma micro catchment. Description of the Assignment The overall objective of this procurement is to competitively select and contract qualified vehicle rental or leasing service provider(s) capable of providing reliable, safe, well-maintained, and appropriately insured vehicles to support the implementation of the NbS4Water Africa – Ethiopia Awash Project. The selected service provider(s) will provide vehicles based on the operational requirements of IUCN. Scope of Work The selected service provider shall provide vehicle rental and/or lease services to IUCN in accordance with the agreed requirements and on a call-off basis, as and when required. The services may include, but are not limited to, the following: Vehicle Provision The selected service provider shall provide safe, reliable, well-maintained, and roadworthy vehicles that meet IUCN’s operational and field-activity requirements. Vehicles shall be suitable for both urban and off-road travel and shall comply with all applicable Ethiopian legal, safety, registration, insurance, and roadworthiness requirements. Vehicle Condition and Standards The primary vehicle category required under this procurement is: Toyota Hilux Double Cab 4x4 – 2.8L Diesel, model year 2020 or newer. title: Physiotherapist
description:
The Physiotherapist is responsible for the treatment, counselling, preventative care and rehabilitation of the motor function and physical wellness of the patients. is responsible for assessing, planning, implementing, and evaluating individualized rehabilitation programs for patients with limb loss and other mobility impairments. Working within a multidisciplinary team, the Physiotherapist facilitates functional recovery, promotes independence, optimizes prosthetic use, and improves patients’ quality of life through evidence-based rehabilitation practices The Physiotherapist tasks and responsibilities include, but are not limited to, the following points: Undertake a comprehensive and accurate assessment of patients in a variety of settings; Identify, plan and manage physiotherapy interventions and rehabilitation plans Provide physio treatments to achieve identified outcomes and monitor patients’ conditions, both for in-patients and out-patients, if needed; Perform all the tasks related to the physio competence framework; Establish, maintain and conclude therapeutic interpersonal relationships with patients and their relatives, based on respect, dignity and care; Conduct comprehensive physical assessments of patients with upper and lower limb amputations, including musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiovascular, balance, gait, and functional evaluations. Provide pre-prosthetic rehabilitation, including: residual limb care and shaping, edema management, scar management, pain management (including phantom limb pain where appropriate), range of motion and strengthening exercises, contracture prevention Cardiovascular conditioning Deliver prosthetic rehabilitation, including: prosthetic gait training, balance and coordination training, functional mobility training Stair negotiation and community ambulation Transfers and activities of daily living (ADL) training Fall prevention strategies Monitor patient progress and modify treatment plans according to clinical outcomes. Encourage patients to have a positive attitude towards physiotherapy by motivating them; Organizing daily group activities, if possible, for patients; Promote an environment that enables patient’s safety and health implementing all necessary actions such as infection control practices, bed sores prevention practices and maintaining high level of hygiene also ensuring physio material are properly cleaned; Ensure that the equipment is functional and well maintained and stored; Ensure documentation/record is accurate and physio chart is properly filled, maintaining confidentially of information; Compiling and submitting periodic reports, if requested, following EMERGENCY guidelines; Be compliant with EMERGENCY guidelines for the treatment of patients; Work closely with prosthetists/orthotists during prosthetic prescription, fitting, alignment, and follow-up. Participate in training programs or activities, meeting timelines and deliverables, if requested by EMERGENCY; Train new staff, if needed. title: Economic Programming and Private Business Partnerships Advisor
description:

Today, PIN stands as one of the largest organizations of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe, supporting vulnerable communities in Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe. PIN empowers civil society, advocates for human rights, and promotes social inclusion both at home and abroad. PIN is present in Ethiopia since 2003, works in partnership with communities, local organisations and public institutions to support sustainable development and improve people’s well-being across the country. Through integrated programming, PIN combines immediate assistance with longer-term, systems-oriented approaches aimed at strengthening resilience, expanding access to essential services and economic opportunities, and enabling locally led solutions. Guided by its Relief and Development strategy, PIN operates across multiple regions and works with a diverse portfolio of institutional donors and partners. About the role: The Economic Programming and Private Business Partnerships Advisor will play a central role in shaping and strengthening People in Need Ethiopia’s economic and private business programming portfolio. The position combines strategic oversight, programme delivery support (with the EU Empower project as a current priority), partnership development, and external positioning, with a strong focus on identifying new opportunities, building relationships, and supporting the design and growth of market-relevant interventions across the Country Programme. While grounded in market systems thinking, the role goes beyond technical advisory to support business engagement, adaptive programming, resource mobilisation, and the translation of programme learning into wider strategic opportunities. Main Duties & Responsibilities: Economic Strategy & Opportunity Development Continuously scan the economic landscape to identify new opportunities, emerging sectors, and partnership potential relevant to the Ethiopia CP’s strategic priorities and programming areas Develop and refine the Ethiopia CP’s approach to economic programming, ensuring interventions are grounded in market realities, responsive to emerging opportunities, and positioned for sustainable impact across the portfolio Lead structured market and sector assessments, translating findings into actionable strategic directions, programme adaptation, and the development of new initiatives across the CP. Facilitate access to finance for target groups and market actors, brokering relationships with banks, microfinance institutions, and impact investors to develop tailored financial products and instruments. Drive youth and women's integration into priority value chains, focusing on value-added participation, distribution roles, and entrepreneurship pathways. We currently work in 73 countries, supporting data-driven decision making in government, advancing evidence-based public health policies, and mounting strategic communication campaigns. Vital Strategies’ priorities are driven by the greatest potential to improve and save lives. They include non-communicable disease prevention, tobacco control, road safety, obesity prevention, overdose prevention, environmental health, and vital statistics systems building. Our programs are primarily concentrated in low- and middle-income countries in Africa, Latin America, Asia and the Pacific. Please visit our website at www.vitalstrategies.org to find out more about our work. Vital Strategies is committed to building a diverse, equitable and inclusive (DEI) organization. We believe our programs are strengthened when they are developed and supported by individuals with diverse life experiences, whose understanding of social and cultural issues can help make our work and workforce more inclusive. We welcome applications from people of all backgrounds. Lead Poisoning Prevention Program: Vital Strategies is expanding our program that addresses the issue of lead poisoning in low- and middle-income countries. We plan to build upon existing efforts and interest by collaborating with governmental agencies in countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America to strengthen health systems and build local expertise in childhood lead exposure to enact sound, cost-effective policies to address exposures. Job Purpose: The position of Government Relations Advisor, Africa will facilitate regional exchange and coordinate high-level engagement and partnership building for the Lead Poisoning Prevention Program across multiple countries in Africa. The role will focus on managing and strengthening relationships with key government and program partners, stakeholders, facilitating regional exchanges and strategy development, and ensuring program alignment with countries’ priorities and global objectives. The incumbent will work closely with country teams to support government engagement, partnership building, share updates on implementation progress, and ensure exchange and coordination among government and consortium partners across the regional portfolio. The role will also provide representation at regional events, support policy engagement, and ensure effective collaboration among regional stakeholders and technical partners. It is preferred that this role be based in Ethiopia, on a full-time hybrid schedule, out of Vital Strategies' office in Addis Ababa, but we are also open to qualified candidates from Ghana, Rwanda, and Tanzania.
